name: Spironolactone for hair loss

card.summary: An oral antiandrogen prescribed off-label, mainly to women, to slow androgen-driven hair thinning and help preserve scalp density.
card.note: Prescription-only; antiandrogen effects make it unsuitable in pregnancy and cause feminising effects in men.

quick.overview:
Spironolactone is a prescription steroid medication originally used for heart failure, high blood pressure and fluid retention. It also blocks androgen receptors to a degree, which is why dermatologists prescribe it off-label for female pattern hair loss, acne and excess facial or body hair.
The appearance payoff is hair preservation: by dampening androgen signalling at the follicle, it is used to slow thinning and keep density, often alongside minoxidil. Wikipedia describes the supporting evidence for hair loss as tentative and low quality, and a 2024 systematic review of androgenic alopecia treatments covered oral, topical and procedural options broadly [1][2].
quick.how: It is taken by mouth under a prescriber's supervision, usually for months before any change in shedding or density is judged, and is frequently combined with topical or oral minoxidil. Clinicians typically check blood potassium and blood pressure. Some men on looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a second-line option behind finasteride or dutasteride, and discuss topical spironolactone mainly for acne and skin texture on steroid cycles [3].
quick.risks: Common effects include menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, dizziness and increased urination; high potassium (hyperkalaemia) is the main serious risk [1]. In men the antiandrogen action can cause breast enlargement and sexual side effects, which is why long-term use in men is generally avoided [1]. It is not used in pregnancy.

lead: Spironolactone is a steroidal medication that blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor and, more weakly, blocks the androgen receptor [1][4]. Its licensed uses are cardiovascular and renal, but dermatologists also prescribe it off-label for androgen-related conditions, including female pattern hair loss, hormonal acne and excess facial or body hair [1].

The appearance goal is hair preservation. In androgen-sensitive scalp follicles, androgens such as DHT shorten the growth phase and shrink the follicle over successive cycles, so hairs come in finer and shorter. By occupying the androgen receptor, spironolactone is used to slow that miniaturisation and help keep density, usually in women and often alongside topical or oral minoxidil [1][5]. Wikipedia describes the supporting evidence for female pattern hair loss as tentative and low quality [1]; Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes small studies and observational reports of improved density and reduced shedding during treatment [4].

In men the same antiandrogen action causes feminising effects such as gynecomastia, so long-term oral use is not usually prescribed. In the RALES heart-failure trial, 9.1% of men on 25 mg/day developed breast enlargement versus 1.3% of controls [1][7]. Male hair-loss discussion online therefore centres on finasteride and dutasteride, with spironolactone raised as a lesser option, and topical spironolactone discussed mainly for acne and skin texture [3].

chain: Blocks androgen receptors in the scalp
angle.text: Used off-label, mostly by women, to slow androgenetic thinning and help keep density, often alongside minoxidil. Men generally use other agents because of feminising effects.

paras: Female pattern hair loss typically presents as diffuse thinning over the top of the scalp with the frontal hairline largely preserved; most affected women have normal testosterone levels [5]. Spironolactone appears in Wikipedia's list of treatment options alongside minoxidil, finasteride and bicalutamide [5]. Wikipedia describes it as a direct but weak androgen receptor antagonist rather than mainly a testosterone-lowering drug [1].

Dermatology practice commonly judges response over many months. Wikipedia reports that response in hirsutism takes up to about six months and in acne one to three months [1]. Grokipedia reports clinical descriptions of a plateau after roughly a year, which it says may prompt combination therapy, and of temporary increased shedding some months after stopping [4].

subs.h: Combination with minoxidil and other agents
paras: Prescribers often pair an antiandrogen with a growth-stimulating agent, since the two act by different routes: minoxidil acts on the follicle's growth cycle, while spironolactone reduces androgen signalling [5]. Wikipedia's female pattern hair loss article notes that combinations of finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole performed better than any single agent in cited work [5]. A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies on androgenic alopecia found that many oral, topical and procedural treatments, including oral minoxidil, finasteride and dutasteride, promoted hair growth [2].

subs.h: Acne, hirsutism and other appearance uses
paras: Spironolactone is also prescribed for hormonal acne in women; the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline addresses systemic therapies including hormonal agents [6], and a 2025 review of acne innovations covers systemic options [11]. Wikipedia calls it a first-line antiandrogen for hirsutism, with effectiveness comparable to finasteride and flutamide in most comparisons [1]. The same article notes use in transfeminine hormone therapy as an antiandrogen [1]. A 2026 editorial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology is titled "Spironolactone rules" [12].

Spironolactone is classed as a steroidal antimineralocorticoid and weak antiandrogen [1]. Its androgen-receptor blockade acts at the target tissue, so measured testosterone may not reflect its benefit [1]. Grokipedia also describes inhibition of 5-alpha-reductase and of testosterone synthesis as contributing effects [4].

Oral bioavailability is 60 to 90%. The parent compound has a half-life of about 1.4 hours, while its active metabolites, including canrenone, persist for roughly 14 to 17 hours, which is why the drug can be dosed once daily [1]. It is poorly water-soluble, so only oral and topical forms have been developed [1].

Menstrual irregularity is the most frequent effect in women and is dose-dependent: about 20% at 50 to 100 mg/day versus about 70% at 200 mg/day, with normal cycles usually returning within about two months of stopping, according to Wikipedia [1]. Birth-control pills often control it [1]. Breast tenderness, dizziness, headache, nausea and increased urination are also reported [1].

High potassium is the main serious risk. In heart-disease patients on typical doses, 10 to 15% develop some hyperkalaemia, with risk concentrated in older people, kidney impairment, and use with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs or potassium supplements [1]. In young women taking it for acne, Wikipedia says significant hyperkalaemia is rare and routine monitoring may be unnecessary [1]. A 2025 randomised trial studied a potassium binder for managing hyperkalaemia during spironolactone optimisation in heart-failure patients [9].

Gynecomastia is the best-known effect in men: Wikipedia cites rates of 30% at 100 mg/day and 62.5% at 200 mg/day in healthy men, usually regressing after stopping but potentially becoming irreversible after about a year [1]. Sexual dysfunction and, at very high doses, reduced sperm count are also reported [1]. Wikipedia notes eplerenone lacks antiandrogenic effects and is more suitable for long-term use in men [1]. T Nation's gynecomastia thread lists spironolactone among medications associated with breast enlargement [15].

Spironolactone crosses the placenta, and it is not recommended in pregnancy because of a theoretical risk of feminising male fetuses; a 2019 systematic review found insufficient evidence either way, and antiandrogens are used in women of reproductive age with adequate contraception [1]. Rare severe skin and blood reactions have been reported [1]. Wikipedia reports five cases of breast cancer in long-term users without establishing a causal link [1]; Grokipedia states that breast-carcinoma warnings were removed from US labelling in 2018 [4].

Spironolactone was discovered in 1957 and introduced in 1959 [1]. Grokipedia attributes its synthesis to chemists John Cella and Robert Tweit at G.D. Searle & Company and gives early 1960 for US approval, and places the start of off-label dermatologic prescribing in the 1980s [4]. It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and is a widely prescribed generic [1].

The heart-failure RALES trial, published in 1999, reported reduced mortality in severe heart failure, and Wikipedia reports about a 30% reduction in death from any cause [1][7]. Later trials examined resistant hypertension (PATHWAY-2, 2015), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (2014), and acute myocardial infarction (2025) [8][10][14].

It is prescription-only in the US, UK and EU [1]. Brand names include Aldactone (tablets), Carospir (oral suspension) and Aldactazide (with hydrochlorothiazide) [1]. Topical 2% and 5% creams (Spiroderm) were sold in Italy in the early 1990s for acne and hirsutism and were discontinued in 2006 after spironolactone was added to Italy's doping list, according to Wikipedia [1]. A T Nation thread quoting a natural-bodybuilding rulebook lists prescription diuretics, including spironolactone, among restricted substances [16].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On looksmax.org a user promoted topical spironolactone cream or gel for acne and skin texture during steroid use, argued that topical application does not disturb hormone levels, and said oral spironolactone can help DHT hair loss but that dutasteride or finasteride are better [3]. T Nation posters have discussed topical spironolactone for back acne, spironolactone alongside growth-hormone use to counter water retention, and spironolactone as part of gynecomastia management [17][18][15].

Randomised trials of spironolactone concentrate on cardiovascular disease: RALES in severe heart failure, TOPCAT in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, PATHWAY-2 and a 2025 comparison with amiloride in resistant hypertension [7][10][8][13]. For hair loss, evidence cited by Wikipedia is limited to tentative, low-quality studies in female pattern hair loss [1]. Grokipedia cites a 2023 retrospective analysis of 67 women in which 49% of those on spironolactone alone showed improved follicular density, and a review reporting hair-count gains of about 10 to 20% over 6 to 12 months with spironolactone alone or with minoxidil; [4]. A 2024 systematic review covered androgenic alopecia treatments broadly [2].

timeline.event: Spironolactone is discovered at G.D. Searle & Company [1][4].
Off-label dermatologic use for androgen-related skin and hair conditions begins to be reported, per Grokipedia [4].
RALES trial reports reduced mortality in severe heart failure [7].
Topical spironolactone (Spiroderm) discontinued in Italy after addition to the doping list [1].
PATHWAY-2 trial establishes spironolactone as the most effective add-on for drug-resistant hypertension [8].
Breast-carcinoma warnings removed from US labelling, per Grokipedia [4].
Systematic review of 141 studies maps oral, topical and procedural treatments for androgenic alopecia [2].

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums spironolactone appears mainly as an anti-acne and anti-DHT adjunct, discussed more for skin than for hair [3].

claims.claim: Oral spironolactone helps DHT-driven hair loss
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says oral spironolactone helps with DHT hair loss but that dutasteride or finasteride are better overall [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the evidence for female pattern hair loss as tentative and low quality; men are generally not given long-term high-dose treatment because of feminising effects [1].

claims.claim: Topical spironolactone counters steroid-related acne without affecting hormones
claims.believers: The thread's author argues topical application does not disturb hormone levels and helps skin texture [3].
claims.experts: Dermatology guidelines address systemic and topical acne therapies but do not cover this topical use in steroid users [6].

claims.claim: Spironolactone is a gentle option for women's thinning that works best with minoxidil
claims.believers: Dermatology-minded users describe pairing an antiandrogen with minoxidil to both stop loss and regrow density [3][5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the evidence for spironolactone in female pattern hair loss as tentative and low quality, while noting combination regimens outperformed single agents in cited work [1][5].

claims.claim: Stopping spironolactone brings the thinning back, sometimes with a shed
claims.believers: Patients and clinicians describe benefits as lasting only while treatment continues, with a temporary shed reported some months after stopping [4].
claims.experts: Grokipedia says data on discontinuation effects are lacking and evidence is mainly observational [4].

claims.claim: Men can use it for hair without feminising side effects
claims.believers: Some forum posters mention oral spironolactone as an experiment behind finasteride or dutasteride [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports gynecomastia in 30% of healthy men at 100 mg/day and says high doses are not recommended in men [1].

claims.claim: Topical spironolactone gives antiandrogen benefit without hormonal effects
claims.believers: A looksmax.org author argues topical application leaves hormone levels alone and improves steroid-related skin [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes topical products were sold in Italy until 2006 and no topical hair-loss trial is described there; Grokipedia says no topical formulation is FDA-approved [1][4].

claims.claim: Spironolactone counters water retention and bloat from other drugs
claims.believers: A T Nation poster listed it as a way to reduce aldosterone-driven fluid retention during growth-hormone use [18].
claims.experts: Wikipedia identifies its core action as aldosterone blockade and lists hyperkalaemia as its main serious risk [1].
